content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a learning-based Contrastive adversarial Loss (CALoss) to train a reconstruction-related task network without the predefined matching rules. CALoss learns to evaluate shape differences by combining the contrastive constraint with the adversarial strategy. It proposes to use contrastive constraint to help CALoss learn shape similarity, and introduce the adversarial strategy to help CALoss mine differences between reconstructed results and ground truths. Experiments on reconstruction-related tasks show CALoss can help task networks to improve reconstruction performances and learn more representative representations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+: The idea of using learning-based contrastive adversarial loss is good and seems to work well.
+: Experiments are good.

-: The paper needs to be more polished in writing. e.g. it refers foldingnet as folding.
-: technically, the perturbations seem only add some variations to the original shape. How about large changes, e.g. including topoloy changes? I didn't see these kinds of examples or discussions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall the general idea is clear. Using contrastive adversarial loss by learning could offer advantages beyond the traditionally used chamfer distance of EMD. The writing can be further polished. I am not confident of the novelty, as it seems similar ideas have been proposed for point cloud processing such as classification/recognition. Also, I do have questions about the effectiveness of the proposed perturbation methods to generate a wide range of sample data for training.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall it is an interesting paper with promising potential. The current version does not seem fully complete both in writing and in the methodology though. I would hope the authors can keep working on these to make the work more convincing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a learnable loss for deep representation learning of 3D shape, which is verified its effectiveness on both tasks of unsupervised classification of point clouds and point cloud completion.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
strength
+ simple yet effective 
+ generic and readily application to other related topics

weakness
- writing should be polished, especailly the abstract and introduction
- limited novelty. The proposed loss could be popular in self-supervised representation learning of 3D shape. pls clarify the main differenece between the proposed one and existing ones. 
- Lack of sufficient comparative evaluation with existing self-supervised representation learning algorithms
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
As mentioned, the novelty of this manuscipt is very marginal, compared to a number of recent self-supervised representation learning of 3D shape. Moreover, the following statement need to be further clarified:
1. less appropriate definition of unsupervised classification -- no labels are used for auto-encoder based representation learning, while training a SVM desires semantic labels. so, the classifier for point clouds is obtained in a supervised learning manner
2. as stated in the paper " As the predefined matching rules are static and unlearnable, training results of CD and EMD may fall into inappropriate local minimums where the shapes are obviously different but with small point-to-point CD/EMD distances". pls give an example to make it easy to understand. In the reviewer's opinion, larger point-to-point CD/EMD distances cannot ensure small shape difference due to point density. However, large shape difference always lead to large CD distances, although there exists approximation error on point sets with CD distance of object shape. 
3. which case will cause unexpected local minimums (in the second item of the contributions)?
content.summary_of_the_review: Although experiment results can support the claim of using the proposed CALoss, considering limited novelty and less precise statement in the manuscript, current version of this paper is not ready for publishing.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a method for calculating the loss function used in point cloud reconstruction. The proposed method makes use of 1D convolutions to learn features from 3D point clouds. The learnt features are then pooled to create global features, on which three different losses are defined. The proposed method was experimented with three different tasks including point cloud reconstruction, unsupervised classification, and point cloud completion. Experimental results on benchmark datasets strongly support the proposed method, and also show its superiority over traditional geometric losses, e.g., Chamfer distance loss, earth mover's distance loss.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
A. Strength
- The studied problem is interesting, and novel (to my understanding)
- The paper is well-written and easy to follow
- The proposed solution is well-motivated
- Experimental results are convincing

B. Weaknesses
- Although improved performance is proven, there is lack of insightful explanation on the improvement gained by the proposed method (see detailed comments in the summary section).
- More discussion on the design of the MLP used in Eq (6) should be provided (see detailed comments in the summary section).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
A. Clarity: the presentation is clear enough.

B. Quality: the proposed method is well-motivated, and the design of loss functions is reasonable.

C. Novelty: the studied problem is novel.

D. Reproducibility: the work could be reproduced if more implementation details are provided.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Although improved performance is proven on a variety of tasks, there is lack of experiments and/or insightful explanation on the improvement gained by the proposed method. For instance, take point cloud reconstruction as a case study, it is obvious to see the impact of a Chamfer distance loss on the task network (via back-propagation). Once CALoss is used to replace Chamfer distance loss, the range of the CALoss may be different from that of the Chamfer distance loss as the CALoss is calculated in the feature domain (not spatial domain like Chamfer distance). It is, therefore, not obvious to see how the change in the CALoss affects the parameters of the task network during back-propagation. To better explain this, the authors may want to investigate the convergence (e.g., convergence speed or number of iterations) when training the task networks in downstream tasks with and without using the CALoss. 

Another way to understand the success of the CALoss is to find its relationship with the Chamfer distance (i.e., relationship between a metric in high-dimensional space and a metric in 3D space). For instance, the authors may show the co-variance of the Chamfer distance and CALoss, i.e., if two shapes are similar (or even identical), their Chamfer distance would be small and the CALoss should also be small. To showcase the limitation of the Chamfer distance, the authors could choose shapes belonging to different classes but having small Chamfer distance and large CALoss.

The authors should also discuss about the design of the MLP used in Eq (6). Since there is a free space for such the design, the authors should explain their chosen design and empirically prove its performance over other choices.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a novel deep learning based adversarial loss (CALoss) to supervise the training of point cloud (PC) reconstruction related neural networks. The proposed method utilizes neural networks to map the input PCD into feature space and represent it as feature vector C_pcd. Given any PC (S_o), its naive ground truth S_g, and perturbed ground truth S_p, the CALoss calculate three loss functions defined in the feature space C_pcd and backpropagate the loss to update network parameters. By attaching CALoss to different PC-related architectures, re-training the new variants, and evaluating their results, the proposed method shows good robustness to reduce errors in varying tasks, including PC reconstruction, completion, and unsupervised classification.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
+ The algorithm is well-explained and easy to follow.
+ The proposed method seems to work well on different tasks, including PC reconstruction, completion, and classification.

Weakness:
- Some essential technical details are missing. For instance, what's the dimension of \delta in Eqn.7? Is it a scalar or a vector? What are and how do set the hyperparameters \epsilon and \epsilon_w in Eqn. 9? Why N_sigma in Eqn.9 is called dynamic  coefficient? Does it mean that the weight will be updated during the training? If yes, how? If no, how do you choose the best value? Regarding network training, what's the optimizer and the total number of epochs you used to train different networks? When comparing with other networks, how many epochs do you use to train each of them, and how you can ensure that the compared networks are converged? In addition, according to the ablation study (Section. 4.7), it seems like the most important part in CALoss is the perturbation term L_p, and the regularization term \epsilon, can you provide some explanation and analysis of why it is so? If you add the \epsilon square term into the loss L_C, I guess that it will enforce \epsilon to be zero, and thus collapse C_g to sum(F_g) according to Eqn. 7. This will further lead to doubts about the effectiveness of the Adaptive pooling and pooling controller (Section. 3.2), which is a major contribution of this paper. I would like to suggest the author conduct an additional ablation study by replacing C_g with sum(F_g) to claim this ambiguity.
- The experiment part is not well organized. For instance, in Section. 4.2, what do you mean by "apply AE and Folding in multiple local regions acquired following PointNet ++"? How do you reconstruct these "local feature-based" LAE and LFolding? In Section. 4.3, what's the metric used to get Table 2? 
- Copied a large amount of content directly from the paper "Learning to Train a Point Cloud Reconstruction Network without Matching" (ECCV 2022). For instance, the related work Sec. 2.2 is almost identical to Sec. 2.1 in the referred paper. In the experiment part, there's large overlapping content in the Sec. 4.1 in this paper and Sec 4.1 in their paper. The author should refer to this paper and rewrite the copied content.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
As explained above, I thinks there's still a big space for the paper to improve w.r.t. writing and clarity.

Except that the proposed method looks slightly different from the referred paper [1], the authors shouldn't directly copy the content without making any changes. I believe that it has been severely against the originality code of ICLR. 

[1] Huang, Tianxin, Xuemeng Yang, Jiangning Zhang, Jinhao Cui, Hao Zou, Jun Chen, Xiangrui Zhao, and Yong Liu. "Learning to Train a Point Cloud Reconstruction Network Without Matching." In European Conference on Computer Vision, pp. 179-194. Springer, Cham, 2022.
content.summary_of_the_review: In summary, this paper presented a novel loss term for point cloud reconstruction related tasks. However, due the insufficient clarification and large amount of direct copied content, I will reject this paper.

content.title: Contrastive Adversarial Loss for Point Cloud Reconstruction
content.TL;DR: Learn a point cloud reconstruction loss by contrastive constraint and adversarial training
content.abstract: For point cloud reconstruction-related tasks, the reconstruction losses to evaluate the shape differences between reconstructed results and the ground truths are typically used to train the task networks. The Chamfer Distance (CD) and Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) are two widely-used reconstruction losses, which firstly use predefined strategies to match points in two point clouds and then apply the average distances from points to their matched neighbors as differentiable measurements of shape differences. However, the predefined matching rules may deviate from the real shape differences and cause defective reconstructed results. To solve the above problem, we propose a learning-based Contrastive adversarial Loss (CALoss) to train a reconstruction-related task network without the predefined matching rules. CALoss learns to evaluate shape differences by combining the contrastive constraint with the adversarial strategy. Specifically, we use the contrastive constraint to help CALoss learn shape similarity, while we introduce the adversarial strategy to help CALoss mine differences between reconstructed results and ground truths. According to experiments on reconstruction-related tasks, CALoss can help task networks improve reconstruction performances and learn more representative representations.
